oneLine: The floor the four games live on: one wallet on a Rust server, a Next.js shell that frames each game, and a postMessage protocol so a game joins by implementing one file rather than by being rewritten.
status:
Built and verified end to end. The shell, the floor and all four games run together; a browser walkthrough sits down at craps, checks the wallet arithmetic, resumes an open table, cashes out, then plays fourteen real spins on the slot and confirms the shell's figure matches the server's to the cent and that the ledger holds exactly three rows (SIGNUP, BUY_IN, CASH_OUT) with the audit balanced.

What is NOT verified here: stages 1 and 2 of casino/Dockerfile (the Node and Rust builds inside Docker). They fail in this sandbox because build containers cannot complete a TLS handshake through its intercepting proxy -- corepack cannot fetch pnpm, cargo cannot reach crates.io. Both stages are exactly the commands that succeed on the host. Stage 3, the runtime image, IS verified: built from the host artifacts, it runs as uid 10001, the binary is PID 1, every route answers 200, the Docker healthcheck reports healthy, and SIGTERM triggers the graceful drain. Run `docker compose build casino` somewhere with ordinary network access before trusting the image.

None of the four games' engines changed. Their suites pass with the same counts as before the casino existed: craps 220, blackjack 187, three card poker 119, Dragon's Shrine 129.

whatWasBuilt.protocol: casino/protocol/ -- the one contract. protocol.ts is the message types and the envelope, client.ts is a game's end, host.ts is the floor's, mode.ts answers 'am I on the floor' synchronously at module load. Vendored into all five apps by tools/sync-protocol.mjs, with a --check mode that fails on drift.
whatWasBuilt.server: casino/server/ -- Rust, Axum, SQLx, SQLite. Players, opaque hashed bearer tokens, an append-only ledger, table sessions, a comp, two leaderboards, a ticker, a WebSocket feed, an audit endpoint, and static hosting for the shell and every game so the casino is one origin. 28 integration tests through the real Router.
whatWasBuilt.shell: casino/shell/ -- Next.js static export. The lobby (tiles, wallet HUD, ticker, boards, cage log, comp), the cage (buy-in and top-up in chips), and play/page.tsx, which is the only screen that brokers money. 25 tests, 21 of them driving a real client against a real host through fake windows.
whatWasBuilt.gameLinks: One file per game: src/lib/casino/link.ts. Takes the buy-in, reports the position, closes off the actions that create money from nowhere, and shouts about a jackpot. Mounted by a FloorLink component in each root layout. Plus persistKey() on each store's storage name and CASINO_BASE_PATH in each next.config.ts.
whatWasBuilt.packaging: casino/Dockerfile (three stages, one image), casino/Dockerfile.dockerignore, casino/docker-compose.yml included from the root compose file, and tools/build-casino.mjs which builds all five apps with the right base paths.

stack.server: Rust 2021, axum 0.8, tokio, sqlx 0.8 (sqlite, runtime-checked queries), argon2, uuid, tracing
stack.shell: Next.js 16.3.2, React 19.2.8, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, zustand 5, vitest
stack.database: SQLite, WAL, integer cents throughout. Portable to Postgres: every query is a runtime-checked string.
stack.protocol: postMessage, JSON, one envelope with a namespace, a version and a direction
stack.fonts: Orbitron, Inter, JetBrains Mono -- self-hosted by next/font at build time, because the CSP allows no remote origins
stack.money: integer cents everywhere except inside the craps engine, which is whole dollars; the craps link converts at the boundary and carries the remainder
stack.ports: casino 8090; the four standalone game containers keep 8080-8083

commands.serverLint: cd casino/server && cargo clippy --all-targets && cargo fmt --check
commands.shellChecks: cd casino/shell && pnpm run typecheck && pnpm run lint
commands.shellDev: cd casino/shell && NEXT_PUBLIC_FLOOR_URL=http://localhost:8090 pnpm dev   # with KNOTZ_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:3010 on the floor

architecture.theModel: Chips at a table. Sitting down debits the wallet and the amount becomes the session's `chips` (one BUY_IN row). While seated the game reports what it holds and the floor writes it to the session -- no ledger row, no wallet movement, because chips moving around a table have not crossed the cage. Standing up moves the chips back (one CASH_OUT row) and closes the session. Walking away does nothing: the chips stay on the table and the lobby offers them back.
architecture.whyFrames: Each game is a finished app with its own build, store, physics and audio graph. A casino that imported them would have to make all four agree on React version, bundler config, CSS layer order and animation budget, and the first disagreement would be paid for in how the games feel to play. So each is hosted exactly as it is, in a frame, and money crosses as messages -- which is also how a real casino integrates a vendor's cabinet.
architecture.whoIsAuthoritative: The client is the authority on the outcome of a round; the server is the authority on everything that crosses the cage -- what a buy-in cost, what a cash-out paid, what the wallet holds, and that a session cannot pay out twice. That is the right trade for play money and the wrong one for real money. A real-money deployment moves each engine behind the API and has the game render a result it was given; the protocol is shaped so that is a change of who calls the engine, not of what the floor looks like.
architecture.dataFlow: game store -> link.ts -> client.ts -> postMessage -> host.ts -> play/page.tsx -> POST /sessions/{id}/sync -> sessions table. Coalesced twice: 120ms in the game (a slot in turbo settles several times a second) and 500ms in the shell (that is where it becomes a database write). The server drops anything at or below the sequence it has applied.

keyDecisions: The protocol is vendored, not imported. Every app builds from its own folder with its own Dockerfile whose context IS that folder, so a workspace package would be invisible from inside every one of those builds. Drift is made a test failure instead: `casino:check` runs first in the build script.

The shell gets client.ts as well as host.ts, which is the one asymmetry in the sync tool. Not for running -- it is the only app holding both ends, so it is the only place the protocol can be tested as a protocol. handshake.test.ts is the reason.

Cents on the wire. Three games already think in cents; craps thinks in whole dollars because a layout is priced in dollars and every payout floors to one exactly as a stickman would. The craps link converts and CARRIES the sub-dollar remainder -- held, never bet, never shown, added back at cash-out.

Two save files per game, chosen at module load by persistKey(). Without it a rack funded by the casino's wallet gets written into the save a standalone visit reads back. The question has to be answerable synchronously because a zustand store picks its storage name when it is created.

Casino mode is detected as framed AND flagged (?casino=1). Framed alone is somebody else embedding the game, which should get the standalone game and no wallet. Flagged alone is a pasted URL with no floor behind it.

A game must not move money before `hello` arrives, and must fall back to its own bankroll if it never does. Standalone is the DEFAULT and the casino is the special case -- which is what keeps all four games independently playable.

CASINO_BASE_PATH is a build input, not a proxy rule. A static export bakes its base path into every asset URL it emits, so a bundle built for / and served from /games/craps/ asks for /_next/... and gets the shell's index.html back: a blank page with no error anybody can see.
One origin, one container. Splitting the shell off would make every postMessage cross-origin, put CORS in front of the wallet, and hand each game frame a browser's third-party storage rules to fight.

The wallet HUD leads with the TOTAL (wallet plus every chip on every table), not the spendable balance. A HUD that led with the balance would drop by a thousand dollars the moment somebody sat down and read as having lost a thousand dollars. Buying in does not make you poorer.

Both card tables report their position only in the betting phase. Mid-round the money is in four or five places with different settlement rules, and deriving 'what does the cage owe' from there means a second implementation of the engine's settlement, out where it can disagree with the first. Cost: a tab dying mid-hand returns the wager -- which is what a table called off mid-hand does.

The two card tables spread one stack across the open boxes and re-level when the player opens or closes one -- between rounds only, with nothing in any spot, and only ever because the player asked. A real table works the same way: chips in front of you, spread over your circles.

The concourse is deliberately not a felt. All four games are warm rooms; the space between them is black glass and cold neon so that walking into a game feels like stepping out of a corridor. Cyan is the house, magenta is a win, gold is money -- everywhere.
Opaque hashed tokens rather than JWTs. The floor hits its database on every request anyway, so the only thing a stateless token would buy is the inability to revoke one.
A guest is a real player row with a real wallet and no password, and `claim` upgrades that row rather than creating a second one. It keeps the wallet, the history and every open table.
The comp is on a timer UNLESS the player is flat broke, in which case it is immediate. A play-money casino that locks a broke player out for eight hours has lost them.

The audit endpoint checks three identities and deliberately not a fourth. Chips do NOT tie back to the ledger: a player who runs a thousand to nine has eight thousand in chips the ledger never saw, because the game's engine created them. That becomes real at cash-out, in one row.
WAL plus BEGIN IMMEDIATE on every money path. See gotchas -- the second one is a correctness fix, not a tuning knob.

The leave button has a 2.5s backstop. A game that implements cash-out replies in a frame or two; one that cannot never replies, and a button that hangs forever on that is worse than one that pays out the server's last position.

The frame gets `allow-scripts allow-same-origin` and nothing else. No top-level navigation, no popups, no forms -- a game has no business doing any of them, and the frame not being able to navigate the top window is what stops a compromised game taking the player anywhere.

The host validates event.source against the frame's contentWindow, which is the check a page that merely knows our origin cannot spoof. Origin alone is not enough: a sibling frame, an opener and an extension content script all share it.

Numbers from a frame are gated on Number.isInteger and a plausible range. NaN, Infinity, a negative, a float off the integer grid and a string are all bugs rather than balances, and the ledger is the last place any of them should turn up.

The server's catalog is a static Rust array, not a table. Adding a game is a literal and a build line; there is no admin UI to build and no migration to write, and the figures in it are the ones each game's own simulation suite measures.
Static export for the shell, same as the games. The floor's binary serves it, so the deployment shape is identical and there is no Node in production anywhere.

The ticker is a CSS marquee with the content rendered twice and a -50% translate. No JavaScript, one transform on one element -- because there is a game running at sixty frames in a frame beside it and the main thread is not ours to spend.

The Counter component tweens with requestAnimationFrame rather than a CSS transition, because there is no CSS property whose interpolation you can read back out as text. A wallet that climbs reads as winning; one that snaps reads as a page re-rendering.

Dialogs use the platform's <dialog> and showModal(), which gives focus trapping, an inert backdrop, Escape and the top layer for free -- and the top layer is the only thing that reliably paints above an iframe running a game with its own stacking contexts.
gotchas: casino/Dockerfile.dockerignore is named that ON PURPOSE. The build context is the repository root but the Dockerfile lives in casino/, and Docker looks for a plain .dockerignore beside the CONTEXT root -- so one in casino/ is silently ignored and BuildKit ships the whole working tree. Measured at 5.4 GB and about a minute before the first instruction ran. BuildKit prefers <dockerfile>.dockerignore when it is there.

SQLite's default BEGIN is deferred, so a read-then-write transaction has to upgrade its lock -- and if another connection holds the write lock SQLite returns SQLITE_BUSY *immediately*, ignoring busy_timeout, because waiting would deadlock. Every money path has that shape, so two concurrent buy-ins produced one success and one 500. db.rs::write_tx uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE. There is a test for the race; do not 'simplify' it back to pool.begin().

The `touch` in the Rust stage of the Dockerfile is load-bearing. Cargo decides what to rebuild from mtimes, and the stub main.rs used to cache the dependency layer already produced a binary newer than the sources copied in afterwards. Without the touch the image ships the stub, which starts, exits zero, and looks like a crash loop with no error message.

The casino client arms its retry interval BEFORE sending the first hello, and the order matters. A host that answers synchronously would otherwise run stopHandshake() before those variables were assigned, clear nothing, and leave the interval armed with the handshake already complete -- a game shouting at a floor that seated it, forever. A browser's postMessage is always async so it cannot happen in production; the protocol test delivers synchronously and caught it.
Both ends of the protocol capture `window` at construction rather than reading the global at use. Same object in a browser; a leaked listener anywhere else, and untestable either way.

cashedOut() flushes any pending position BEFORE sending the final count. Without that, a win inside the coalescing window goes out with a higher sequence number than the cash-out and the server's staleness guard drops the newer figure. There is a test.
A broke position (chips === 0) is never coalesced away -- it goes out immediately. 120ms of ambiguity between 'you are out of chips' and nothing happening reads as the game being broken.

React's compiler lint is on in the shell and it is strict about three things this app kept doing: setState in an effect to mirror other state (derive it), Date.now() during render (useNow()), and effects that re-seed a dialog's fields (key the component instead). All three complaints were correct; do not reach for eslint-disable.
useSearchParams in a statically exported route needs a Suspense boundary. The page is prerendered at build time when there is no URL to read.

The craps store's addChips and newSession, and the card tables' rebuy/newSession/setSeatOccupied, are REPLACED by each link via setState. That is why they are captured into an `original` object first. Outside the casino every one of them is correct; inside it the first two mint money.
Craps' newSession is also what sets sessionStarted, which is how the link skips the setup screen. Do not 'optimise' it to a bankroll poke.
The craps link carries `chips % 100`. If you change how it funds the table, carry it or the player silently loses up to 99 cents per top-up.
The two card tables re-level only when `quiet(table)` -- betting phase, nothing in any circle. Re-levelling with chips down would move a live wager.

FloorLink is mounted in each game's ROOT LAYOUT, not its page. Craps and the slot both gate their page on a start screen, and the link is what makes that screen unnecessary on the floor -- so it has to be mounted before the page decides what to render.
Each game's next.config.ts reads CASINO_BASE_PATH. Building a game by hand for the casino without it produces a blank page with no console error.

The floor's CSP allows NO remote origins. Adding a CDN script tag anywhere will be blocked silently. wasm-unsafe-eval is there for one reason: the craps dice are a Rapier solver compiled to WebAssembly.
X-Frame-Options is SAMEORIGIN, not DENY. DENY would break the casino; ALLOWALL would let anybody wrap our games in their own chrome and take the bets.

The WebSocket token is in the query string because a browser WebSocket cannot send an Authorization header. That is the same trade every WebSocket API makes; the exposure is a proxy log rather than the wire.

The leaderboard's effect depends on the player's handle, and not only for the 'you' marker: the first load races the guest sign-up, so without it a brand new visitor's first screen says 'nobody has bought in yet' while showing them five thousand dollars.
The live dot in the wallet HUD is on the label row, not beside the total. Next to the figure it reads as a decimal point.
play/page.tsx guards its auto-resume with a ref. The effect's inputs change as the wallet moves, and a second POST /sessions would take a second buy-in for a table that is already open.
Ticker rows are written by other players' games and arrive over a socket. They are narrowed in floor.ts (asTicker) and clipped before they reach the DOM as text. Never render one as markup.

The catalog's `path` must equal /games/<slug>/ and the slug must equal the directory under KNOTZ_GAMES_DIR and the slug in the build script. A test asserts the first; the other two are conventions the build script makes true.
A dev build of the shell against a separately-run floor is the ONLY configuration that needs KNOTZ_ALLOWED_ORIGINS. In production the floor serves the shell and there is no CORS layer at all.
`docker compose down -v` destroys every wallet. That is why it is the longer command.

verification.serverTests: 28 integration tests through the real Router with real migrations: signup, buy-in, resume, bust-and-rebuy, replayed sync, no-ledger-rows-on-sync, cross-tenant refusal, negative positions, double cash-out, stale and newer final counts, top-up, the comp, claim, handles, logout, catalog shape, ticker, leaderboard, session-token scope, a four-game crawl, and two buy-ins racing for the last chips.
verification.protocolTests: 21 tests driving a real client against a real host through fake windows: the handshake and its retry, standalone fallback, wrong-slug refusal, foreign-window refusal, echo and noise rejection, coalescing, the immediate broke position, the staleness guard, seven implausible numbers, cash-out ordering, post-close refusal, top-up, busy/need-chips/leave, an over-long label, ping/pong, dispose, and a resumed table.
verification.gameSuites: craps 220, blackjack 187, three card poker 119, Dragon's Shrine 129 -- the same counts as before the casino existed. Plus typecheck, lint and a production build on all five apps.
verification.browserWalkthrough: Playwright against the real binary serving the real builds: four tiles, the opening stake, the cage, seating at craps with the felt showing the casino bankroll and the setup screen skipped, the wallet arithmetic (5000 total / 4000 free / 1000 on tables), the open table offered back on the floor, cash-out from the lobby, and the slot showing its buy-in. No console errors.
verification.realPlay: Fourteen spins on Dragon's Shrine through the frame: the server recorded 14 rounds and $14 of action, chips moved to $1,986.12, the shell's bar agreed to the cent, cash-out paid $1,986.12 into the wallet, the ledger held exactly SIGNUP/BUY_IN/CASH_OUT, and /api/v1/audit came back balanced.
verification.runtimeImage: Stage 3 of the Dockerfile built from host artifacts: 170MB, runs as uid 10001, knotz-floor is PID 1, every route 200, Docker healthcheck healthy, SIGTERM logs 'last call -- draining'.
verification.notVerifiedHere: Stages 1 and 2 of casino/Dockerfile. Build containers in this sandbox cannot complete a TLS handshake through its intercepting proxy, so corepack cannot fetch pnpm and cargo cannot reach crates.io. Both stages run exactly the commands that succeed on the host. Run `docker compose build casino` with ordinary network access before trusting the image.

openItems: Run `docker compose build casino` somewhere with ordinary network access. Stages 1 and 2 are unverified for the reason above.
Rate limit POST /api/v1/auth/guest. It hands out a wallet to anybody who asks, as often as they ask.
Postgres. Every query is already a portable runtime-checked string; what is missing is a second migration set and a connection-string branch in db.rs.
The floor has no admin surface. A comped correction is an ADJUST row applied by hand over SQL, which is why the ledger kind exists.
Craps still has a second seat in its state (solo mode never lets it bet). A future two-player casino table would want the floor to seat both, which the protocol does not model.
The card tables' per-seat drawdown chart is re-based when boxes are opened or closed. Harmless for a single-box player; a combined session chart in the shell would be the honest fix.
The session token is issued, hashed and checked, and GET /api/v1/table is the only endpoint that uses it. A game that outgrows the frame would want more.
No pause/resume is sent to a game when a dialog covers it. The protocol has the messages; the shell does not send them yet.
The ticker never shows a bust, even though the protocol has the kind. Deliberate for now -- a floor that announces losses is a floor nobody plays.
Achievements, a VIP tier that does anything, and a tournament mode are all unbuilt. The tier column exists.
No service worker, so the shell is installable but not offline-capable. A wallet-backed casino offline is arguably wrong anyway.
The audit endpoint needs any valid token. It reports on every player, naming none beyond an id, but it should probably need more than a guest's.

repoNotes.principle: Games do not share a build and share no code. The casino does not change that: it adds a protocol they all vendor, and the vendoring is checked rather than trusted.
repoNotes.theOnlySharedThing: casino/protocol/, copied into five apps by tools/sync-protocol.mjs. Edit the canonical copy and run `pnpm run casino:sync`.
repoNotes.whatDidNotChange: Every engine, felt, paytable, animation and audio graph in all four games. The diff in each game is: one link module, one FloorLink component, one import and one call in its store's persist name, one basePath block in next.config.ts, and the vendored protocol.
repoNotes.thePredictionThatWasWrong: The old root README predicted that merging these tables into one casino would mean merging their chrome and keeping the felts. It is built the other way round: nothing was merged, the duplicated chrome is load-bearing because it is what makes each game a room, and the casino is deliberately not one of them.

pickUpHere.readFirst: casino/README.md for the model and the plug-in contract; casino/protocol/protocol.ts for why it is a message protocol at all; casino/server/src/sessions.rs for where the trust boundary sits.
pickUpHere.toAddAGame: A link module (copy the closest of the four), a Game literal in casino/server/src/catalog.rs, a line in casino/tools/build-casino.mjs, and persistKey() on its store. Nothing in the shell and nothing in the server.
pickUpHere.beforeTouchingMoney: cd casino/server && cargo test. It finishes by folding the ledger back up and comparing. If a change can make that fail, the change is wrong.

deployment.shape: One container: a Rust binary, the built shell, the four built games, and a SQLite file at /data.
deployment.port: 8090. The four standalone game containers keep 8080-8083 and still work.
deployment.state: Everything worth keeping is the one SQLite file. It is the only path the container writes to, which is what lets the root filesystem be read-only.
deployment.volume: The one thing to get right. A container host with an ephemeral filesystem and no volume at /data resets every wallet on every deploy.
deployment.scaling: One instance until Postgres. SQLite is a file; two instances with their own copies are two casinos that disagree.
deployment.reverseProxy: Needs the WebSocket upgrade passed through (the live wallet feed) and a long read timeout. Do not cache /api/v1 -- the floor already sets no-store, and a proxy that ignores it will serve one player another player's balance.
deployment.migrations: Run at boot from the binary. No separate step, no window where schema and binary disagree.
deployment.backup: sqlite3 .backup, which is safe against a running writer. A file copy of a WAL database can catch a torn write.

pwa.installable: Yes -- casino/shell/public/manifest.webmanifest, display: fullscreen, which matters for a game that owns the whole viewport.
pwa.icon: One SVG at public/icon.svg, used as the favicon, the maskable icon and the home-screen tile, so they cannot drift.
pwa.walletIsPerDevice: A guest's token lives in that browser's localStorage, so a phone and a laptop are two players with two bankrolls. Claiming the account joins them and keeps the wallet and every open table.
pwa.offline: No service worker. Deliberate: the wallet is on the server and a casino without it is not a casino.
pwa.viewport: maximumScale 1 on purpose. A game frame is the whole viewport and manages its own scale; pinching the shell around it leaves a game half off screen with no way back.
